steps.say: At the very bottom of the cord, a tumour of the tail filament causes backache and bladder trouble in young adults. Removing it whole cures the patient, while cutting it up seeds the spinal fluid. Whole removal is the whole cure.
steps.tx: **Myxopapillary ependymomas** (tail-filament tumours) of the **filum terminale** (cord tail strand) present with low back pain and sphincter disturbance. **En bloc resection** (whole-piece removal) is curative, while piecemeal removal seeds the canal, so the operation plans one intact specimen rather than internal debulking from the start.

steps.say: Inside the cord itself, two tumours look similar but behave oppositely. The central one with rust caps at its poles peels out cleanly, while the off-centre infiltrating one is biopsied and radiated. The scan's symmetry decides the operation.
steps.tx: Intramedullary **ependymomas** (central cord tumours) sit centrally with a **cap sign** (rust-coloured pole caps of old blood) and a clear plane, favouring gross total resection. The **eccentric astrocytoma** (off-centre infiltrating tumour), by contrast, gets biopsy plus radiotherapy, since chasing it through normal cord costs more function than the tumour itself.

steps.say: Nerve-sheath tumours of the spine grow through the bony exit hole and take an hourglass shape. Taking the whole joint to free them can bend the spine later, so surgeons rebuild with screws. Most are benign and cured by complete removal.
steps.tx: **Schwannomas** (dorsal-root sheath tumours) arise from **dorsal roots** (sensory nerve roots) as enhancing **dumbbell schwannoma** (hourglass exit-hole lesions) widening the foramen. Large ones need **facetectomy fusion** (joint removal plus screws) after resection to prevent deformity, since removing the joint that frees the tumour also removes the spine's local stability.

steps.say: The commonest benign cord-covering tumour favours middle-aged women in the chest spine. It carries a tail on its covering and squeezes the cord from behind. Opening from the back, removing it and sealing its base cures the leg weakness in most cases.
steps.tx: Thoracic **spinal meningioma** (cord-covering tumour) with **dural tails** (covering flares) in middle-aged women is resected posteriorly with **dural coagulation** (base sealing) or patch. Removing the tumour and its attachment cures **myelopathy** (cord-pressure weakness) in most cases, since these benign pills of tissue compress rather than invade.

vis.alt: H and E stained histology of a meningioma, showing woven to trabecular architecture, whorls, psammoma bodies, syncytial cells with eosinophilic cytoplasms, and round uniform nuclei.
vis.caption: Meningioma whorls and psammoma bodies: the benign histology behind thoracic tumours. Credit: Mikael Haggstrom, via Wikimedia Commons.

steps.say: Some brain tumours are shedding cells down the spinal fluid that coat the cord in sugar-like icing. Staging such a child means imaging the whole spine and brain plus testing the fluid itself. Finding those drops changes treatment from local to whole-axis.
steps.tx: **Drop metastases** (fallen tumour seeds) from medulloblastoma and ependymoma coat the cord with **sugar coating** (icing-like seed layer), staged with full craniospinal MRI and **CSF cytology** (fluid cell test) at diagnosis. Positive seeds convert treatment from local surgery to whole-axis radiation and chemotherapy covering brain and spine together.

steps.say: Cancers of the primitive spine remnant at the sacrum return relentlessly unless removed in one bony block. Scooping from inside guarantees regrowth, so surgeons lift the whole segment and follow with proton beams for dirty edges. Half measures fail here.
steps.tx: Sacral **chordomas** (notochord-remnant cancers) and chondrosarcomas need wide **en bloc spondylectomy** (whole-segment removal) because intralesional surgery recurs. **Proton therapy** (stopping-beam radiation) follows for positive margins, since these gelatinous tumours seed every plane the knife opens and only intact margins cure.

steps.say: Round-cell cancer of the spine in the young is treated like its limb counterpart: drugs first, then surgery and radiation. A gene test confirms the diagnosis before the first needle. Adult spread deposits, by contrast, get separation surgery plus focused radiation.
steps.tx: **Ewing sarcoma** (young round-cell cancer) of the spine gets **neoadjuvant chemotherapy** (drugs first) with **EWSR1** (defining gene test) testing, then surgery plus radiotherapy. Adult metastases instead get separation surgery plus SBRT, since Ewing's chemosensitivity earns a drugs-first strategy that spread deposits cannot use.

steps.say: Bright red knots with flow gaps and fluid cavities mark the inherited form of cord tumour. They are cured by sealing the feeders first and removing the knot, and every case triggers screening of the whole family. Relatives may carry the same gene silently.
steps.tx: **Haemangioblastomas** (blood-knot tumours) with **flow voids** (vessel gaps) and syrinx in **VHL** (von Hippel-Lindau) disease are resected curatively with devascularisation first. **VHL screening** (family gene testing) follows every associated lesion, since relatives carry silent tumours of kidney, eye and adrenal that screening catches early.
